los.text: Recall the rationale for contact tracing and chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal disease
los.html:
• Neisseria meningitidis is carried in the nasopharynx (about 10% of adults, peaking in teenagers and young adults) and spreads by respiratory droplets and close contact.
  • Close contacts of a case have a much higher risk of disease (hundreds of times the background rate), mostly in the first 7 days, because they share the same strain (often carried by someone in the household).
  • Chemoprophylaxis eradicates carriage within the close-contact network, preventing secondary cases; it's given as soon as possible (ideally within 24 h).
  • Public health: meningitis and meningococcal disease are notifiable on clinical suspicion (don't wait for confirmation) to the health protection team (UKHSA; Public Health Wales), who trace contacts, arrange prophylaxis and offer vaccination if the strain is vaccine-preventable (A, C, W, Y; sometimes B in clusters).
  • Index case: needs carriage eradication before discharge unless treated with ceftriaxone (or ciprofloxacin).

los.text: Describe how to determine the need for chemoprophylaxis in individuals in contact with a case of meningococcal disease.
los.html:
Who gets prophylaxis (contact in the 7 days before onset)Who doesn't (usually)
Household contacts: living or sleeping in the same household, including students sharing a kitchen in halls, boarding school dormitoryClassroom, nursery or work contacts (unless a cluster: health protection team decides)
Intimate kissing contactsFriends, social contacts
Healthcare workers whose mouth or nose was directly exposed to respiratory secretions (e.g. airway management, suction) without a maskHealthcare staff with routine contact
Passengers in very close prolonged contact (case-by-case)
  • Drugs:
DrugNotes
Ciprofloxacin single oral dose (adult 500 mg)First choice for all ages, including pregnancy
Rifampicin twice daily for 2 daysInteractions (reduces the contraceptive pill, warfarin), orange-red urine, tears and contact lenses
Ceftriaxone single IM doseAlternative (e.g. pregnancy)
  • Give prophylaxis up to 4 weeks after the case's onset; give written information about symptoms to watch for.

los.text: Identify the key symptoms and signs of encephalitis and investigate appropriately
los.html:
• Encephalitis = inflammation of the brain parenchyma, so the key feature is altered mental state (unlike meningitis, which mainly causes headache and neck stiffness; both can coexist: meningoencephalitis).
Symptoms and signs
Fever, headache
Confusion, behaviour or personality change, reduced consciousness
Seizures (focal or generalised)
Focal neurology: dysphasia, hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsies
Psychiatric features, memory loss, olfactory or gustatory hallucinations (temporal lobe)
  • Investigations: blood cultures, FBC, CRP, glucose, U&E (SIADH), HIV
    • CT if contraindications to LP
    • lumbar puncture (opening pressure, cells, protein, glucose with paired plasma, PCR for HSV-1/2, VZV, enterovirus)
    • MRI brain (best imaging)
    • EEG (encephalopathy, temporal discharges, non-convulsive status)
    • autoimmune antibodies (serum and CSF) if infection screen is negative.
  • Start IV aciclovir immediately on suspicion (don't wait for tests).

los.text: Identify the CSF changes consistent with viral encephalitis
los.html:
CSFViralBacterialTB
AppearanceClearTurbidClear or fibrin web
White cellsRaised, lymphocytes (5–1000/µL)Very high, neutrophilsRaised, lymphocytes
ProteinNormal or mildly raisedHighVery high
Glucose (CSF:plasma)Normal (>0.6)Low (<0.4)Very low
OtherPCR positive; red cells in HSV (haemorrhagic necrosis)Gram stain, cultureAFB stain, culture, PCR
  • Caveats: very early viral CSF can show neutrophils or be normal (repeat LP if suspicion remains)
    • prior antibiotics change bacterial CSF.

los.text: Identify the main symptoms and signs of Herpes Simplex Encephalitis, select appropriate investigations and plan treatment
los.html:
• HSV encephalitis: most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis
    • usually HSV-1 (reactivation) in adults
    • affects the temporal and frontal lobes (often asymmetrical).
FeatureDetail
SymptomsFever, headache, confusion, behaviour change, seizures, dysphasia, memory loss, olfactory/gustatory hallucinations, reduced consciousness
CSFLymphocytes, mildly raised protein, normal glucose, red cells; HSV PCR (gold standard)
MRITemporal lobe (and insular/inferior frontal) high signal and swelling
EEGTemporal slowing or periodic lateralised discharges
Treatment
  • IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg three times a day for 14–21 days, started immediately
  • Adjust for renal function and keep hydrated (crystal nephropathy)
  • Repeat LP/PCR before stopping if needed
  • Manage seizures and raised ICP
  • Supportive care.
OutcomeUntreated mortality ~70%; treated ~10–20%, with many survivors left with deficits.

los.text: Identify the common complications of HSV encephalitis
los.html:
Complication
Memory impairment (amnesia from hippocampal damage), cognitive deficits
Behaviour and personality change, mood disorders
Epilepsy
Dysphasia
Autoimmune (anti-NMDA receptor) encephalitis after HSV (~20%, weeks later; new psychiatric or movement symptoms)
Acute: raised ICP, status epilepticus, SIADH, aspiration pneumonia, death
  • Rehabilitation: neuropsychology, OT, SALT; support for families.

los.text: Recall other causes of encephalitis, both infective and antibody mediated, and select appropriate investigations
los.html:
CauseClues
VZVShingles rash, immunosuppression, vasculitis/stroke
EnterovirusesChildren, summer, often meningitis
EBV, CMV (immunosuppressed), HIV
Measles (SSPE years later), mumpsUnvaccinated
Travel/vector-borne: rabies, Japanese, tick-borne, West NileTravel, animal bites, ticks
Bacterial: Listeria (rhombencephalitis), TB, Mycoplasma, syphilis
Toxoplasma, CryptococcusHIV
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitisYoung women; psychiatric symptoms, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, reduced consciousness; ovarian teratoma
Anti-LGI1 encephalitisOlder men; faciobrachial dystonic seizures, memory loss, hyponatraemia
Paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, anti-Ma2)Small-cell lung cancer, testicular cancer
ADEMChildren after infection or vaccination; multifocal demyelination
Investigations
  • CSF PCR panel and culture
  • Serum and CSF autoantibodies
  • MRI
  • EEG
  • HIV and syphilis serology
  • Tumour screen (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, pelvic/testicular ultrasound or MRI).
Autoimmune treatmentSteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, tumour removal; rituximab second line.

los.text: Describe when it is safe to undertake a lumbar puncture
los.html:
• Lumbar puncture helps confirm meningitis/encephalitis and identify the organism, but never delay antibiotics (and aciclovir) for LP or CT
    • aim to do LP within 1 hour of arrival if safe.
Delay LP / CT first ifWhy
  • Signs of raised ICP: reduced or fluctuating consciousness
  • Focal neurological signs
  • Papilloedema
  • New focal or prolonged seizures
  • Bradycardia with hypertension
  • Abnormal pupils or posturing
Risk of brain herniation (coning); a normal CT doesn't fully exclude this risk
Shock / haemodynamic instability, respiratory compromiseStabilise first
Coagulopathy (low platelets, deranged clotting, anticoagulants)Spinal haematoma
Skin infection at the LP siteIntroducing infection
Extensive purpura (meningococcal sepsis)LP adds little; resuscitation is the priority
ImmunocompromiseHigher risk of mass lesions: CT first

los.text: Identify the main bacterial and viral pathogens affecting the CNS in different age groups and link them to why the infections differ in those age groups.
los.html:
AgeMain bacteriaWhy
Neonates (<3 months)Group B Streptococcus, E. coli (K1), Listeria monocytogenesAcquired from the maternal genital and GI tract at birth; immature immunity (complement, neutrophils, no own IgM/IgA)
Infants and young childrenN. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, (H. influenzae type b, now rare)Waning maternal antibody; under 2s respond poorly to polysaccharide capsules (T-independent antigens)
Teenagers and young adultsN. meningitidis (+ pneumococcus)Carriage peaks at ~19; crowding (halls), kissing, smoking
AdultsS. pneumoniae (commonest), N. meningitidisPneumococcal spread from otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia, skull fracture (CSF leak)
>60, immunocompromised, pregnancy, alcoholS. pneumoniae, ListeriaWeak cell-mediated immunity (Listeria is intracellular)
VirusesEnteroviruses (commonest cause of meningitis overall), HSV-2 (recurrent meningitis), VZV, mumps, HIV seroconversion. Others: TB, Cryptococcus (HIV).
Empirical treatment(NICE NG240)
  • Ceftriaxone IV
  • Add amoxicillin for Listeria risk (<3 months, >60, immunocompromised)
  • Add vancomycin if recent travel to areas with resistant pneumococcus
  • Dexamethasone in adults and children over 3 months with suspected bacterial meningitis (reduces hearing loss and neurological sequelae, especially pneumococcal)
  • Under 3 months: cefotaxime + amoxicillin.
  • In the community: benzylpenicillin IM/IV before transfer for suspected meningococcal disease.

los.text: Link the use of specific vaccines to specific indications, intended outcomes and side effects.
sessions: Diagnosis, treatment, sequelae, prevention intracranial infections
los.html:
VaccineIndication / intended outcomeSide effects
Hib (conjugate, in the 6-in-1)Infants: prevents H. influenzae b meningitis and epiglottitis (now rare)Local reactions, fever
MenB (4CMenB)Infants (and at-risk groups): MenB is the commonest UK serogroup in infantsFever (common): give prophylactic paracetamol with infant doses
MenACWY (conjugate)Teenagers (~14) and university freshers under 25; travel (Hajj); aspleniaLocal reactions; reduces carriage → herd immunity
Pneumococcal conjugate (PCV)Infants; at-risk groupsFever, irritability; serotype replacement
Pneumococcal polysaccharide (PPV23)≥65 and at-risk (asplenia, CKD, chronic lung/heart/liver disease, diabetes, immunosuppression)Local reactions; weaker in under-2s
MMR (live)Prevents mumps meningitis, measles encephalitis (and SSPE)Fever and rash at 7–10 days, parotitis, febrile seizures, rarely ITP; no link with autism
BCG (live)At-risk infants: protects against TB meningitis and miliary TB in childrenLocal ulcer, scar, lymphadenitis
  • Conjugate vaccines link a polysaccharide to a carrier protein → T-cell-dependent response with memory, effective under 2 years, and they reduce carriage (herd immunity).
  • Asplenia/hyposplenism: pneumococcal, MenB, MenACWY, Hib, annual flu; lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis may be advised.
  • Live vaccines are avoided in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy.

los.text: Link pathological changes in the cranial cavity with symptoms, signs and complications.
sessions: Diagnosis, treatment, sequelae, prevention intracranial infections
los.html:
Pathological changeSymptoms, signs and complications
Inflammation of the pia–arachnoid, pus in the subarachnoid spaceHeadache, neck stiffness, photophobia; Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs (stretching inflamed roots); bulging fontanelle in infants
Cerebral oedema (vasogenic, cytotoxic, interstitial) → raised ICPVomiting, reduced GCS, seizures, papilloedema (late), Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) → herniation (uncal: fixed dilated pupil; tonsillar: coning)
Impaired CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations, or obstructionHydrocephalus (communicating or obstructive)
Vasculitis and venous sinus/cortical vein thrombosisInfarcts, focal deficits, seizures
Exudate around cranial nerves; cochlear inflammationCranial nerve palsies (VI, III, VII), sensorineural hearing loss (commonest long-term complication: audiology within 4 weeks)
Subdural collections, brain abscessPersistent fever, focal signs (especially infants)
ADH releaseSIADH (hyponatraemia)
Meningococcal septicaemiaEndotoxin → capillary leak, DIC, non-blanching purpuric rash, purpura fulminans, shock, adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen).
Long-termHearing loss, epilepsy, cognitive and learning problems, limb loss (septicaemia), hydrocephalus.

los.text: Identify, describe and label the three layers of meninges: the dura mater, the arachnoid mater, and the pia mater and the important structures relating to them.
los.html:
LayerStructureSpaces and features
Dura materTough outer layer; two layers in the skull, one in the spineExtradural space (potential in the skull, real in the spine with fat and veins); dural venous sinuses between its layers
Arachnoid materThin, avascular, lies against the duraSubdural space (potential; bridging veins cross it); arachnoid granulations project into the sinuses (CSF absorption)
Pia materDelicate, follows every sulcus; carries vesselsSubarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia: CSF, cerebral arteries; cisterns where it widens
  • Spinal cord: pia forms denticulate ligaments (anchor the cord laterally) and the filum terminale
    • cord ends at L1/2, dural sac at S2.
BleedSpaceVessel
ExtraduralBetween skull and duraMiddle meningeal artery (pterion)
SubduralBetween dura and arachnoidBridging veins
SubarachnoidUnder the arachnoidBerry aneurysm (circle of Willis), trauma
  • Meningitis inflames the arachnoid and pia (leptomeninges) and the CSF in between.

los.text: Describe the endosteal and meningeal layers of the dura mater, the four septa created by it dividing up the cranial cavity, and the relationship with the major venous sinuses (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, diaphragma sellae).
los.html:
• Cranial dura: endosteal layer (the periosteum of the skull, continuous with pericranium through foramina) and meningeal layer (continuous with the spinal dura).
    • They are fused except where they separate to enclose the dural venous sinuses, and where the meningeal layer folds inwards as septa.
SeptumPositionSinuses in its edges
Falx cerebriSickle between the cerebral hemispheres, attached to crista galli in frontSuperior sagittal (attached edge), inferior sagittal (free edge), straight sinus (where it meets the tentorium)
Tentorium cerebelliTent over the cerebellum, under the occipital lobes; free edge forms the tentorial notch around the midbrainTransverse sinuses (attached edge), superior petrosal sinuses, straight sinus
Falx cerebelliSmall midline fold between the cerebellar hemispheresOccipital sinus
Diaphragma sellaeRoof over the pituitary fossa, pierced by the stalkIntercavernous sinuses
HerniationUncus through the tentorial notch (compresses III → dilated pupil); cingulate gyrus under the falx; tonsils through the foramen magnum.
Nerve supplyDura is pain-sensitive (V above the tentorium, C1–3 and X below): headache.

los.text: Describe the anatomical structures encountered during the following procedures: lumbar puncture, spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthetic block, epidural (peridural) anaesthetic block. Explain the indications and risks associated with these techniques.
los.html:
ProcedureLevelLayers passedNeedle end point
Lumbar punctureL3/4 or L4/5 (Tuffier's line at L4)Skin, fat, supraspinous, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoidSubarachnoid space (CSF drips back)
Spinal (subarachnoid) blockSame, below L1/2SameSubarachnoid space: small dose of anaesthetic mixes with CSF
Epidural blockAny level (lumbar for labour)Up to ligamentum flavum, then loss of resistanceEpidural space (outside the dura); catheter left in
Lumbar punctureSpinal blockEpidural
UsesDiagnose meningitis, SAH (xanthochromia), measure pressure, give drugsCaesarean section, lower limb and lower abdominal surgeryLabour analgesia, post-operative pain relief, surgery
Onset / dosen/aFast, dense, small doseSlower, larger volume, can be topped up
RisksPost-dural puncture headache, infection, bleeding, coning if raised ICP with a mass (CT first)Hypotension (sympathetic block), high block, headacheHypotension, accidental dural tap, epidural haematoma (anticoagulants) or abscess → cord compression, local anaesthetic toxicity
  • Contraindications: raised ICP with a mass lesion, coagulopathy, infection at the site, patient refusal.

los.text: Identify the components of the ventricular system and link to the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid and the functional consequences of obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid drainage.
los.html:
1. ProductionChoroid plexus (mainly in the lateral ventricles), ~500 mL/day; ~150 mL present at any time.
2. Lateral ventriclesInterventricular foramina (of Monro) → 3rd ventricle.
3Cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) in the midbrain → 4th ventricle.
4Median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka) → subarachnoid space (cisterns, around the brain and cord).
5Absorption through arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus (venous blood).
ProblemTypeCauses
Block within the ventriclesObstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalusAqueduct stenosis (narrowest point), colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro, posterior fossa tumours, Chiari malformation
Poor absorptionCommunicating hydrocephalusAfter meningitis or SAH (granulations scarred)
Normal pressure hydrocephalusOlder adults: gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, dementia ("wet, wobbly, wacky")
  • Effects: raised ICP (headache worse lying down and in the morning, vomiting, papilloedema, VI palsy)
    • in infants, an enlarging head and bulging fontanelle (sutures open).
    • Treat with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.
  • Never do an LP when obstructive hydrocephalus or a mass is suspected (risk of coning).

los.text: Assess a patient with tremor and determine if the tremor is Benign Essential Tremor or Parkinsonian
los.html:
FeatureEssential tremorParkinsonian tremor
WhenPostural and action (arms outstretched, finger–nose, holding a cup)At rest ("pill-rolling"), lessens with movement, may re-emerge after a delay on posture
DistributionBilateral, fairly symmetrical; hands, head ("yes-yes"/"no-no"), voiceAsymmetrical at onset; hands, legs, jaw, chin (not head)
Frequency4–12 Hz4–6 Hz
AlcoholImproves itNo effect
Family historyCommon (autosomal dominant)Usually none
Other signsNone (maybe mild gait unsteadiness)Bradykinesia, rigidity (cogwheeling), shuffling gait, reduced arm swing, hypomimia
HandwritingLarge, shakyMicrographia
TreatmentPropranolol, primidoneDopaminergic drugs
Examination
  • Observe at rest (distract: count backwards)
  • Arms outstretched
  • Finger–nose
  • Spiral drawing and writing
  • Finger tapping (decrement = bradykinesia)
  • Tone with synkinesis (activation manoeuvre)
  • Gait.
Other tremors
  • Enhanced physiological (anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, caffeine, alcohol withdrawal, drugs: salbutamol, lithium, valproate, SSRIs), cerebellar intention tremor, dystonic, drug-induced parkinsonism (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), functional.
  • DaTSCAN if unsure (normal in essential tremor).

los.text: Identify the key features of idiopathic Parkinson's disease, including common non-motor symptoms
los.html:
Pathology
  • Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (nigrostriatal pathway) with Lewy bodies (α-synuclein)
  • Symptoms appear after ~50–60% of neurons are lost.
Motor diagnosisBradykinesia (essential: slowness with decrement in speed/amplitude) plus rest tremor and/or rigidity; usually asymmetrical; good levodopa response.
Motor featuresNon-motor features
Bradykinesia, rest tremor, lead-pipe/cogwheel rigidityAnosmia and REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams): often years before motor signs
Shuffling gait, reduced arm swing, festination, freezing, stooped postureConstipation, urinary urgency, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension, drooling
Hypomimia (masked face), hypophonia, micrographiaDepression, anxiety, apathy
Postural instability and falls (later)Cognitive impairment / dementia, hallucinations
Sleep problems, fatigue, pain, seborrhoea

los.text: Recognise ‘red flag’ symptoms that should prompt consideration of a different diagnosis
los.html:
Red flagSuggests
Early falls (first 1–3 years), vertical (downgaze) palsy, axial rigidity, "surprised" stareProgressive supranuclear palsy
Early severe autonomic failure (postural hypotension, urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction), cerebellar signs, stridorMultiple system atrophy
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism, early visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognitionDementia with Lewy bodies
Asymmetric apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss, myoclonusCorticobasal degeneration
Poor or no response to levodopa, symmetrical onset, rapid progression, early severe dysarthria/dysphagiaAtypical parkinsonism
Drug exposure (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)Drug-induced parkinsonism (symmetrical, may reverse on stopping)
Lower-body parkinsonism, step-wise course, vascular risk factorsVascular parkinsonism
Gait apraxia + urinary incontinence + dementiaNormal pressure hydrocephalus
Onset <40, liver disease, psychiatric symptomsWilson's disease (caeruloplasmin, copper, Kayser–Fleischer rings)

los.text: Formulate an appropriate management plan for someone with PD and understand the role of drugs in the treatment of this condition
los.html:
• Refer untreated to a specialist to confirm the diagnosis (clinical; DaTSCAN if uncertain)
    • PD nurse specialist
    • MDT: physio (gait, falls), OT, SALT (speech, swallow), dietitian, psychology, palliative care later.
Drug (NICE NG71)UseKey side effects
Levodopa + decarboxylase inhibitor (co-careldopa, co-beneldopa)First line when motor symptoms affect quality of life; most effectiveNausea, postural hypotension, dyskinesias, wearing-off and on–off fluctuations (long term)
Dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine patch)First line if symptoms don't affect quality of life (alternative), or adjunctImpulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, shopping), excessive daytime sleepiness (driving), hallucinations, oedema
MAO-B inhibitors (rasagiline, selegiline, safinamide)Early or adjunctMild; interactions
COMT inhibitors (entacapone, opicapone)Adjunct for wearing-off (prolong levodopa)Dark urine, diarrhoea
AmantadineDyskinesiasConfusion, livedo reticularis
Apomorphine (SC), levodopa intestinal gel, deep brain stimulation (subthalamic nucleus)Advanced disease
Never stop PD drugs suddenly
  • Risk of parkinsonism–hyperpyrexia syndrome (like NMS) and severe rigidity
  • in hospital they are time-critical (give on time)
  • If nil by mouth use a rotigotine patch or NG route.
Avoid dopamine antagonistsHaloperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine; use domperidone for nausea.
Non-motorDepression (SSRIs), dementia (rivastigmine), psychosis (reduce drugs; quetiapine or clozapine), orthostatic hypotension (midodrine, fludrocortisone), constipation, drooling (glycopyrronium), sleep problems.

los.text: Recognise the key features of other common movement disorders
los.html:
DisorderKey featuresManagement / cause
DystoniaSustained or intermittent contractions → twisting postures (cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, writer's cramp); "sensory trick" relieves itBotulinum toxin; acute drug-induced dystonia (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) → procyclidine
ChoreaBrief, irregular, flowing, dance-like movements
  • Huntington's disease (autosomal dominant CAG repeat, chromosome 4, anticipation; chorea + dementia + psychiatric; tetrabenazine)
  • Sydenham's chorea (post-streptococcal)
  • Drugs (levodopa)
  • Pregnancy
  • SLE
  • Polycythaemia
HemiballismusViolent flinging of one sideContralateral subthalamic nucleus lesion (stroke)
TicsBrief stereotyped movements or sounds, premonitory urge, suppressibleTourette's (motor + vocal tics >1 year, childhood onset); behavioural therapy
MyoclonusSudden shock-like jerksMetabolic (uraemia, liver failure), opioid toxicity, hypoxic brain injury, CJD, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Tardive dyskinesiaOrofacial chewing/lip-smackingLong-term antipsychotics
Restless legs syndromeUrge to move legs in the evening, relieved by movingIron deficiency (check ferritin), pregnancy, CKD; dopamine agonists, gabapentinoids
Drug-induced parkinsonismSymmetrical bradykinesia and rigidityAntipsychotics, metoclopramide: stop if possible

los.text: Describe the main clinical features and principles of management of migraine and cluster headache
los.html:
MigraineCluster headache
WhoWomen > men; often from teensMen > women, smokers, 20–40s
PainUnilateral (or bilateral), throbbing, moderate–severe, worse with activityStrictly unilateral, excruciating, orbital/temporal
Duration4–72 hours15–180 minutes, up to 8 a day, often same time (at night), in bouts of weeks–months
AssociatedNausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia; aura in ~1/3 (visual zig-zags, scotoma, sensory; develops over ≥5 min, lasts 5–60 min)Ipsilateral autonomic: lacrimation, red eye, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, ptosis/miosis, eyelid swelling
BehaviourLies still in a dark roomRestless, pacing
TriggersStress, sleep change, menstruation, missed mealsAlcohol during a bout
Migraine treatment(NICE CG150)
  • Acute: triptan (e.g. sumatriptan) + NSAID or paracetamol, taken early in the headache; antiemetic (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine); avoid opioids. Triptans are contraindicated in IHD, previous stroke and uncontrolled hypertension.
  • Prevention (frequent or disabling attacks): propranolol, topiramate (teratogenic; reduces pill efficacy), amitriptyline, candesartan; acupuncture, riboflavin; CGRP monoclonal antibodies after 3 failed preventives; botulinum toxin for chronic migraine; gepants (rimegepant).
  • Migraine with aura: combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated (stroke risk).
  • Avoid medication overuse headache: limit triptans/combination analgesics to <10 days a month and simple analgesics to <15.
Cluster treatment
  • Acute: 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min, non-rebreather, 15–20 min) and SC sumatriptan 6 mg (or nasal triptan)
  • Oral analgesics don't work.
  • Prevention: verapamil (ECG monitoring for heart block)
  • Bridging with prednisolone or greater occipital nerve block
  • Lithium.
  • Refer to neurology
  • Imaging for first presentation.

los.text: Describe the assessment and management of a person with neuro-ophthalmological symptoms including: double vision, ptosis, visual field defects, painful visual loss, papilloedema
los.html:
SymptomAssessmentKey causes and management
Double visionMonocular (persists with the other eye covered: refractive, cataract) vs binocular (misalignment); direction worst; fatigability; pupils
  • III palsy: eye "down and out", ptosis
  • Dilated pupil = compressive (posterior communicating artery aneurysm: urgent CT angiography)
  • Pupil-sparing = microvascular (diabetes).
  • IV palsy: vertical diplopia worse looking down (stairs), head tilt away.
  • VI palsy: horizontal diplopia worse looking towards the lesion
  • Raised ICP (false localising).
  • Myasthenia (fatigable, variable, pupils normal).
  • Thyroid eye disease.
  • INO (MS)
PtosisComplete vs partial; pupil; fatigabilityIII palsy (with mydriasis), Horner's (partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis: carotid dissection if painful, Pancoast tumour), myasthenia (fatigable), age-related aponeurotic, myotonic dystrophy
Visual field defectsConfrontation, formal perimetry
  • Monocular (optic nerve, retina)
  • Bitemporal hemianopia (chiasm: pituitary tumour)
  • Homonymous hemianopia (post-chiasmal: stroke; macular sparing in occipital lesions)
  • Superior quadrantanopia (temporal), inferior (parietal)
Painful visual lossAcuity, colour, RAPD, fundi, ESR/CRP, eye exam
  • Optic neuritis (young woman, pain on eye movement, red desaturation, RAPD, central scotoma; MS link → MRI; steroids speed recovery)
  • Giant cell arteritis (>50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, high ESR/CRP → immediate high-dose steroids, same-day specialist review, temporal artery ultrasound/biopsy)
  • Acute angle-closure glaucoma (red eye, halos, fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, vomiting → emergency ophthalmology)
  • Uveitis, keratitis
PapilloedemaBilateral disc swelling = raised ICP
  • Urgent imaging (CT/MRI with venography) before LP: tumour
  • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (young, obese women; headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus; weight loss, acetazolamide)
  • Venous sinus thrombosis
  • Hydrocephalus
  • Malignant hypertension

los.text: Identify the classic signs and symptoms of MS
los.html:
• Who: young adults (20–40), women ~3:1, more common further from the equator (vitamin D), smoking, EBV.
Classic features
Optic neuritis (painful monocular visual loss)
Sensory: numbness, paraesthesia, Lhermitte's sign (electric shock down the spine on neck flexion)
Motor: UMN weakness, spasticity, spastic paraparesis
Eye movements: diplopia, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (bilateral INO in a young person strongly suggests MS)
Cerebellar/brainstem: ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus, dysarthria, vertigo
Bladder (urgency, frequency, retention), bowel and sexual dysfunction
Fatigue (very common), depression, cognitive problems, pain
Uhthoff's phenomenon: symptoms worsen with heat (hot bath, exercise)
  • Partial transverse myelitis and trigeminal neuralgia in a young person are other presentations.

los.text: Select appropriate investigations that would enable you to confirm the diagnosis
los.html:
• Diagnosis (McDonald criteria 2017): clinical attacks plus evidence of dissemination in space (lesions in different CNS areas) and dissemination in time (lesions of different ages or a new attack), with no better explanation.
InvestigationFinding
MRI brain and spinal cord with gadoliniumPeriventricular (Dawson's fingers), juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions; enhancing + non-enhancing lesions together = dissemination in time
CSFOligoclonal bands in CSF but not serum (can substitute for dissemination in time)
Visual evoked potentialsDelayed conduction (previous optic neuritis)
Bloods to exclude mimicsB12, TFTs, ANA, HIV, syphilis, ACE (sarcoidosis), aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies (neuromyelitis optica spectrum, MOGAD)

los.text: Describe the main types of disease course
los.html:
CourseFeatures
Clinically isolated syndromeFirst episode (e.g. optic neuritis); MRI lesions predict conversion to MS
Relapsing–remitting (~85% at onset)Relapses (new or worsening symptoms >24 h, without fever or infection, ≥30 days apart) with full or partial recovery
Secondary progressiveAfter relapsing–remitting (many within 15–20 years): gradual worsening, with or without relapses
Primary progressive (~10–15%)Progressive from onset, often older (~40), men and women equally, usually spinal cord (progressive gait problems)
  • Courses are described as active (relapses or new MRI lesions) or not, and progressing or not.

los.text: Describe principles of treatment
los.html:
AimTreatment
Acute relapse (disabling)
  • Exclude infection (e.g. UTI) first
  • Methylprednisolone 500 mg orally daily for 5 days (or 1 g IV for 3–5 days): speeds recovery but doesn't change long-term outcome
Disease-modifying therapy (relapsing MS)
  • Reduce relapses and new lesions: moderate efficacy (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate)
  • High efficacy (natalizumab: PML risk with JC virus; ocrelizumab/ofatumumab (anti-CD20), alemtuzumab, cladribine, S1P modulators such as fingolimod)
  • Autologous stem cell transplant
Progressive MSOcrelizumab (early active primary progressive), siponimod (active secondary progressive)
Symptoms
  • Spasticity (physio, baclofen, gabapentin, tizanidine, botulinum toxin)
  • Fatigue (exercise, CBT, amantadine)
  • Bladder (antimuscarinics for urgency; intermittent self-catheterisation if residual >100 mL)
  • Neuropathic pain
  • Depression
  • Oscillopsia (gabapentin)
MDT and lifestyleMS nurse, physio, OT, SALT, psychology; exercise, stop smoking, vitamin D, vaccinations (before immunosuppression), pregnancy planning

los.text: Identify the precipitants for relapse and disease worsening
los.html:
Precipitant
Infections (UTIs, viral illnesses)
Postpartum (relapse rate rises in the 3 months after birth; falls during pregnancy)
Stress, fatigue, sleep deprivation
Smoking (faster progression)
Low vitamin D
Stopping DMTs (rebound after natalizumab or fingolimod)
Heat (Uhthoff's)
  • Pseudo-relapse: temporary worsening of old symptoms due to infection, fever, heat or stress, lasting <24 h or settling when the trigger is treated: look for and treat infection rather than giving steroids.

los.text: Assess a person presenting with headache and identify the “red flag” features that may indicate a secondary headache disorder
los.html:
Red flag (secondary headache)Think of
Thunderclap (peak intensity within 1 minute)
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage
  • Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction
  • Venous sinus thrombosis
  • Pituitary apoplexy
  • Arterial dissection: CT (sensitive within 6 h)
  • Then LP ≥12 h after onset for xanthochromia if needed
Fever, neck stiffness, rash, confusionMeningitis/encephalitis
New headache over 50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual symptomsGiant cell arteritis
Focal neurology, seizures, personality change, reduced consciousnessTumour, abscess, stroke, haemorrhage
Papilloedema; headache worse lying down, in the morning, on coughing/straining, with vomitingRaised ICP (tumour, IIH, venous thrombosis)
Worse on standing, better lyingLow-pressure headache (post-LP, CSF leak)
Cancer or immunosuppression (HIV)Metastases, opportunistic infection
Pregnancy/postpartumPre-eclampsia, venous sinus thrombosis
Head injury, anticoagulantsSubdural haematoma
Progressive headache, new onset after ValsalvaStructural cause
Red painful eye with halosAcute angle-closure glaucoma
  • Assessment: onset and time course, character, site, triggers, associated features, analgesic use (overuse), contraception and pregnancy
    • examination: BP, temperature, fundoscopy, neurological exam, neck stiffness, temporal arteries, eyes.

los.text: Assess a patient presenting with a primary headache disorder, specifically migraine and cluster headaches and provide a plan for investigation and management
los.html:
Primary headachePlan
Migraine
  • Diagnose on history (no imaging if typical)
  • Headache diary
  • Acute: triptan + NSAID/paracetamol ± antiemetic
  • Prevention if frequent/disabling (propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline)
  • Limit acute medicines (avoid overuse)
  • Lifestyle (sleep, regular meals, hydration, exercise)
  • Check contraception if aura
  • Review
Cluster
  • High-flow 100% oxygen at home (home oxygen order) and SC sumatriptan
  • Verapamil prevention (baseline and follow-up ECGs)
  • Bridging steroids or occipital nerve block
  • Neurology referral and MRI at first presentation
  • Stop smoking, avoid alcohol in bouts
Tension-typeBilateral pressing/tight band, mild–moderate, not worse with activity, no nausea; aspirin, paracetamol or NSAID; acupuncture for prevention
Medication overuseAnalgesics on ≥10–15 days a month: stop the overused drug abruptly (opioids gradually), expect worsening for a few weeks, then reassess
InvestigationsNone routinely for typical primary headache without red flags; image if atypical features or red flags.
Safety-netReturn if the headache changes character, becomes thunderclap, or new neurological symptoms appear.

los.text: Identify the symptoms and signs of common neurological conditions, investigate and manage appropriately
los.html:
ConditionKey featuresInvestigationsManagement
Bell's palsyAcute LMN facial weakness including the forehead, hyperacusis, taste lossClinical; exclude ear vesicles (Ramsay Hunt: VZV)Prednisolone within 72 h; eye protection (lubricants, tape at night)
Guillain–Barré syndromeAscending symmetrical weakness after infection (Campylobacter), areflexia, back pain, autonomic instabilityCSF: high protein, normal cells; nerve conduction; FVC monitoringIVIG or plasma exchange; ICU if FVC falls; VTE prophylaxis
Myasthenia gravisFatigable weakness: ptosis, diplopia, bulbar, proximal limbsAChR antibodies (anti-MuSK), CT chest (thymoma), single-fibre EMGPyridostigmine, steroids, azathioprine, thymectomy; crisis: IVIG/plasma exchange; avoid aminoglycosides, magnesium
Motor neurone diseaseMixed UMN + LMN signs, fasciculations, no sensory loss, eye movements and sphincters sparedEMG, MRI to exclude mimicsRiluzole, NIV, gastrostomy, MDT, palliative care
Peripheral neuropathyGlove and stocking sensory loss, reduced ankle jerksGlucose/HbA1c, B12, folate, TFTs, U&E, LFTs, protein electrophoresis, nerve conductionTreat cause (diabetes, alcohol, B12, drugs such as vincristine), foot care, neuropathic pain drugs
DementiaProgressive cognitive decline affecting functionCognitive tests, bloods for reversible causes, CT/MRIAcetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine), memantine; avoid antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia
Epilepsy, strokeSee weeks 230 and 231

los.text: Describe the assessment and management of a person presenting with dysfunction of the lower cranial nerves, including disorders of the production of speech, swallowing and tongue dysfunction.
sessions: Brain stem dysfunction, including speech and swallowing
los.html:
ProblemFeaturesCauses
Bulbar palsy (LMN, IX–XII)Wasted, fasciculating tongue, absent gag, nasal speech, nasal regurgitation, normal or absent jaw jerkMND, Guillain–Barré, myasthenia, lateral medullary (brainstem) stroke, syringobulbia, skull base tumours
Pseudobulbar palsy (UMN, bilateral corticobulbar)Small, stiff (spastic) tongue, brisk jaw jerk, slow strained ("Donald Duck") speech, emotional labilityBilateral strokes, MS, MND
Dysarthria (articulation)Flaccid (LMN), spastic (UMN), ataxic (cerebellar: slurred, scanning), hypokinetic (Parkinson's: quiet, monotonous)
Dysphasia (language)Expressive (Broca's): non-fluent, comprehension intact; receptive (Wernicke's): fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension; conductive (poor repetition)Stroke, tumour (dominant hemisphere)
Dysphonia (voice)Hoarseness, weak "bovine" coughRecurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (lung cancer, thyroid surgery, aortic aneurysm), laryngeal disease
TongueXII palsy: deviates towards the lesion, wastingSkull base tumour, carotid dissection, MND
PalateX palsy: uvula deviates away from the lesion
Assessment
  • Listen to speech ("baby hippopotamus", "British constitution", "pa-ta-ka")
  • Voice and cough
  • Palate elevation
  • Gag (IX afferent, X efferent)
  • Tongue (wasting, fasciculation, power)
  • Jaw jerk
  • Observe a water swallow
  • Look for wider neurological signs.
Dysphagia
  • Oropharyngeal (neurological) causes coughing or choking on swallowing, nasal regurgitation, wet voice, aspiration pneumonia.
  • SALT assessment, videofluoroscopy or FEES
  • Modified textures (IDDSI levels), thickened fluids, posture
  • NG, then gastrostomy (PEG/RIG) if long term.
ManagementTreat the cause (pyridostigmine for myasthenia; riluzole, early gastrostomy and NIV in MND); communication aids (AAC); dietitian; aspiration prevention.
